Abstract—Motivated by the limited generalization of super-
vised image matching models to unseen image domains, we
explore the zero-shot deployment of DINO features for this task.
The generalist visual representation extracted from DINO has
inherent ambiguity when used to match feature points among
semantically similar instances, prompting us to adopt a many-
to-many (m-to-m) matching paradigm. However, the existing
robust mechanism under m-to-m data association is computa-
tionally heavy, which requires finding a maximum-cardinality
matching in the inlier association graph for each parameter
evaluation. To address this inefficiency, we introduce a novel
likelihood perspective, which interprets the existing method as a
‘zeroth-order’ approximation of otherwise intractable likelihood
calculation, and inspires us to propose a faster and finer-grained
robust mechanism, termed as Harmonic Consensus Maximiza-
tion (HCM). Take camera pose estimation as an exemplifying
downstream task, we demonstrate that general-purpose visual
features, used out of the box without any adaptation, can compete
with specialized matching models on out-of-distribution datasets
when mated with m-to-m association and the HCM mechanism.
I. INTRODUCTION
Image Feature Matching is a longstanding problem in
robotics and computer vision, underpinning critical tasks such
as visual localization [33] and visual-inertial odometry [7].
Classical pipelines established in the 2000s use hand-crafted
features with built-in local invariance [27, 4], and employ
variants of nearest neighbor test for data association. The
advent of deep learning introduced learned features [45, 11] for
greater robustness to appearance variation. Heuristic matching
and filtering methodshave similarly been supplanted by end-
to-end trainable neural models [32, 34, 25],in which attention
mechanisms [40] play a pivotal role in aggregating intra- and
inter-image contextual cues. Detector-free matchers further
eliminate the reliance on keypoints altogether, performing
dense matching across the entire image [38, 41]. Most recently,
MASt3R [23] grounds image matching in 3D by augmenting
a point-map regression model with a dedicated matching head.
Generality Challenge. Despite their strong performance,
supervised matching methods excel primarily within specific
image domains [5]. Models are typically trained on sepa-
rate, domain-specific datasets—for example, on ScanNet [10]
dataset for indoor scenes and on MegaDepth [24] for outdoor
environments. This dependency on large-scale, expensively
annotated correspondence data makes achieving broad do-
main generality a likely enduring challenge. Visual Foun-
dation Models like CLIP [31] and DINO [35] offer a path
toward broad generalization. Trained via self-supervision on
vast image collections without targeting specific downstream
tasks, these models learn versatile and robust general-purpose
features, enabling a single frozen backbone to serve diverse
applications. Recent methods [19, 12, 26] utilize the general
knowledge embedded in these models to guide visual feature
matching. However, with the training process being domain-
aware, the generalizability issue is only partially alleviated [5].
We are motivated by this generality challenge to ask:
Can DINO features be directly deployed for local image
matching, without domain-specific adaptation?
Inherent Ambiguity in Geometric Matching. While zero-
shot deployment of general-purpose visual representations has
shown promise for semantic correspondence [1, 39, 46], these
generalist features exhibit inherent ambiguity when applied
to geometric matching, both within and across object in-
stances [47, 26]. This stems from two primary factors: (a)
the training objective for global image understanding often
conflicts with the demand for high-quality dense feature
maps [35], and (b) geometric association based primarily on
semantic information is naturally ambiguous [20]. Although
the recent DINOv3 model [35] can produce substantially
sharper feature maps, the second source of ambiguity persists.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, the true associations rarely attain the
highest cosine similarity, particularly when multiple instances
or semantically similar object parts are present. Consequently,
we argue that the conventional one-to-one (1-to-1) association
paradigm is ill-suited for deploying DINO in image matching.
Many-to-Many Association. We embrace the ambiguity of
DINO features by accepting multiple candidate associations
for each keypoint, thereby increasing matching recall—albeit
at the cost of reduced precision. This many-to-many (m-
to-m) association paradigm also appears in other estimation
contexts, typically due to specific problem characteristics:
either no prior knowledge of data association is available [30,
6, 42, 43], or quantized feature descriptors lead to indistin-
guishable matches [28, 8, 20]. Our perspective aligns closely
with Fredriksson et al. [15], who relax the nearest neighbor test
to include more potentially correct matches, thereby handling
ambiguous patterns and textures more robustly.
Robust Mechanisms. The underlying 1-to-1 physical con-
straint, e.g., a pixel is the projection of a unique 3D point,
provides valuable prior information but also introduces signif-
icant computational challenges to estimation. Viewed through
graph theory, the data associations form a bipartite graph, and
identifying the real matching corresponds to selecting a subset
of edges without sharing vertices [15]. Heuristically, a param-

Position of this work. We investigate zero-shot deployment
of DINO models [29, 35] for image matching. In contrast
to global understanding tasks like image retrieval [21] and
semantic segmentation [39, 46] where DINO-based zero-
shot methods excel, geometric matching of image features
is inherently less amenable to competing with supervised
models, as it demands both intra- and inter-image reasoning.
Our goal, therefore, is not to outperform specialized models
on established benchmarks. Rather, we aim to identify data
association and estimation paradigms that best unlock the
potential of DINO features in geometric estimation tasks, and
to achieve robust performance on out-of-distribution (OOD)
datasets where supervised models generalize poorly. With this
position in mind, we make four main contributions:
• Advocating many-to-many association. Based on the
inherent ambiguity of DINO features in drawing geomet-
ric correspondence, we advocate m-to-m association to
ensure viability of downstream estimation tasks.
• A Unified Probabilistic Formulation. We frame gen-
eral parameter estimation problems under m-to-m data
association as a maximum-likelihood problem, based on
two assumptions that extend probabilistic justifications
under 1-to-1 matching [2]. We reveal that the exist-
ing method based on Matching Cardinality Maximiza-
tion (MCM) [15] is a zeroth-order approximation to the
otherwise intractable likelihood calculation.
• A fast and accurate robust mechanism. Grounded in
the above probabilistic perspective, we propose a novel
robust mechanism, termed Harmonic Consensus Maxi-
mization (HCM), which features linear evaluation com-
plexity and provides finer granularity in distinguishing
ambiguous hypotheses. In our experiments, it consistently
outperforms the MCM method in speed and accuracy.
• Empirical validation for camera pose estimation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of combining DINO


features with m-to-m association and HCM mechanism
on camera pose estimation. Using only frozen last-layer
features from DINOv2/v3 models and a simple mutual
K nearest neighbor test, our zero-shot pipeline performs
competitively and even better than specialized models like
LightGlue [25] and MASt3R [23] on OOD datasets.
Paper Organization. The remainder of this paper is struc-
tured as follows. Section II formulates general parameter
estimation under m-to-m association and reviews the MCM
mechanism. Section III presents our ML formulation, pro-
vides novel interpretations for MCM, derives and illustrates
our robust mechanism HCM. Section IV details a zero-shot
pipeline that deploys DINO features in image matching with
m-to-m association and HCM. Experimental settings and a
comprehensive discussion of results are provided in Section V.
At last, we discuss future directions and conclude this paper.
II. ESTIMATION UNDER MANY-TO-MANY ASSOCIATION

IV. ZERO-SHOT DEPLOYMENT OF DINOV3 FEATURES
In this section, we introduce our zero-shot pipelines for
deploying DINO features in image matching.
A. Mate DINO Feature with Unsupervised Point Detectors
The vision Transformer (ViT) architecture adopted by DINO
divides an image into patches of a certain size, and all pixels
in a patch share the same representation. In pursuit of a pixel-
level description, we bi-linearly interpolate DINO features at
interest points identified by the SuperPoint model [11], which
is also trained in a self-supervised manner while specialized at
interest point detection and description. We choose the ‘token’
facet from the last layer of DINOv2/v3 models, as suggested
by per-layer analysis on correspondence quality in [46, 35].
Among the family of DINOv3 models distilled from the
gigantic 7B-parameters teacher, we choose the efficient and
widely adopted ViT-L model with patch size 16x16 (ViT-
L/16), which achieves performance close to that of the 7B
model [35]. Similarly, we choose the 14x14 ViT-L model with
registers (ViT-L/14 w/ reg) for DINOv2 [29].
B. Mutual K Nearest Neighbor Association
We generalize the 1-to-1 MNN test to admit top-K mutually
nearest neighbors, termed the MKNN test. On top of simplic-
ity, this approach uniformly bounds the number of potential
associations for each feature, thereby facilitating memory
allocation in implementation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we
compute the Group Precision@5px metric on the NAVI-Multi
and NAVI-Wild datasets [18] with K = 3, 5, 8. This metric
represents the probability that a real association (within a 5-
pixel range of the ground truth matching pixel) is contained in
candidates that pass the MKNN test, and corresponds to hyper-
parameters px and py in Assumption 1. Details regarding the
datasets and a broader quantitative analysis with Precision
and Recall metrics are provided in Section V. The results
based on DINOv3 are presented in Figure 4, which reveal that
(a) adopting a larger K effectively improves group precision
for feature association, and (b) challenging scenarios involving
significant viewpoint changes yield a lower group precision.
C. Marginal Probability Assignment
Marginal probability assignment under Assumption 1 is akin
to finding a assignment matrix P ∈R|S|×|T | with given row
and column sums. This resembles the classic matrix scaling
problem with a strictly positive P, which can be solved by
Sinkhorn’s iterations [36]. However, the assignment matrix
in our problem must adhere to a sparsity pattern dictated
by data associations, and thus a feasible solution may not
exist [37]. To address this, we heuristically relax the strict
row and column sum constraints based on a principle of
uniformity. Specifically, we do not discriminate associations
that pass the MKNN test with cosine similarity. Instead, we
rely on the structure of association graph to regularize the
final assignment. This design choice is predicated on the
observation that due to the general-purpose nature of DINO,

V. EXPERIMENTS
This section evaluates the correspondence quality and cam-
era pose estimation accuracy attained by our zero-shot image
matching paradigm, which combines DINO features interpo-
lated at SuperPoint keypoints with m-to-m association and
the proposed (HCM) mechanism. For camera pose estima-
tion, we compute globally optimal estimates via parallelized
brute-force search and assess their accuracy without any
post-refinement. In Appendix C, we detail our brute-force
search procedure, accelerated by dimensionality reduction
techniques [13] and CUDA parallelization. We emphasize
that the objective of these experiments is not to demonstrate
that zero-shot image matching pipelines can match the perfor-
mance of supervised models on well-addressed benchmarks.
Rather, we aim to validate the efficacy of the ‘m-to-m + HCM’
paradigm by showing consistently better accuracy over the
1-to-1 and MCM counterparts, and by attaining competitive
accuracy on OOD datasets relative to supervised models.
A. Experimental Setup
Baselines. For MNN-based pipelines relying solely on
keypoint descriptors, we compare with SIFT [27], Super-
Point [11], and DINO features interpolated at SuperPoint
keypoints, respectively denoted as SIFT(K=1), SP(K=1),
SP+D2/D3(K=1). For detector-based supervised matchers, we
compare with SuperGlue [34] and LightGlue [25] on top of
SuperPoint keypoints and descriptors, denoted respectively
as SP+SG, SP+LG; and compare with a foundation-model-
enhanced method OmniGlue [19] which integrates SuperPoint
and DINOv2 [29]. For detector-free methods, we compare with
Efficient-LoFTR [41] (ELoFTR). For 3D-grounding methods,
we compare with MASt3R [23].
Datasets. Our evaluation spans three datasets of 1500 test
image pairs and increasing difficulty of generalization:
• ScanNet [10] dataset depicts indoor scenes with view-
point changes and texture-less regions. Following [34],

B. Correspondence Quality
Correspondence quality is evaluated using the metrics of
Precision, Dense Recall, and Success Ratio on the NAVI-
Multi and NAVI-Wild datasets, which provide dense pixel
correspondences between image pairs. A keypoint xi in the
left image is considered correctly matched to a point yj in
the right image if it falls within 5 pixels of the ground-truth
correspondence. This check is performed symmetrically for
keypoints yj in the right image. The final count of correct
associations is the average of these bidirectional checks, and
Precision is calculated as the ratio of this count to the total
number of output correspondences (if no correspondence is
output, Precision is defined as zero). In contrast, Dense Recall
measures association completeness as the percentage of rec-
ognized associations among all ground-truth pixel correspon-
dences. Since the median number of real pixel associations
exceeds 5 million on both NAVI-Multi and NAVI-Wild, we
report Dense Recall in units of 0.001%: note that a 0.001%
difference in Dense Recall corresponds to tens of additional
correct matches. We also report the Success Ratio, defined as
the fraction of image pairs for which the matching method
outputs ≥5 correct associations and thereby enables valid
pose estimation using minimal essential matrix solvers.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
In this work, we investigate zero-shot deployment of DINO
features for image matching and camera pose estimation. We
propose adopting a many-to-many association paradigm in
recognition of the semantic nature of such general-purpose
features. We further propose a novel robust mechanism for
general estimation problems under m-to-m data association,
which is rooted in rigorous likelihood analysis and surpasses
the current method in both speed and accuracy. Evaluation
on three datasets with increasing difficulty of generalization
reveals that zero-shot DINO-based image matching pipelines
can achieve competent and even better performance than
specialized models on OOD image domains, provided they
are equipped with the right association and robust paradigm.
Several promising research directions are motivated by the
results of this paper. First, the probability assignment matrix
output by supervised matching models provides the exact
probabilistic substrate for the proposed (HCM) mechanism.
It would be interesting to evaluate the in-domain and out-of-
domain performance gains for supervised matching models
from selecting m-to-m associations in their output assignment
matrix and using (HCM) for robust estimation. Second, model
tuning based on frozen DINO backbones under the guidance
of the (HCM) mechanism is another interesting direction.

Abstract: Motivated by the limited generalization of super- vised image matching models to unseen image domains, we explore the zero-shot deployment of DINO features for this task. The generalist visual representation extracted from DINO has inherent ambiguity when used to match feature points among semantically similar instances, prompting us to adopt a many- to-many (m-to-m) matching paradigm. However, the existing robust mechanism under m-to-m data association is computa- tionally heavy, which requires finding a maximum-cardinality matching in the inlier association graph for each parameter evaluation. To address this inefficiency, we introduce a novel likelihood perspective, which interprets the existing method as a ‘zeroth-order’ approximation of otherwise intractable likelihood calculation, and inspires us to propose a faster and finer-grained robust mechanism, termed as Harmonic Consensus Maximiza- tion (HCM). Take camera pose estimation as an exemplifying downstream task, we demonstrate that general-purpose visual features, used out of the box without any adaptation, can compete with specialized matching models on out-of-distribution datasets when mated with m-to-m association and the HCM mechanism.
